accepted.question_text: What is a general classification or characterization of geodetic graphs, where a graph is geodetic when every pair of distinct vertices is connected by a unique shortest path (a unique geodesic)?

evidence.quote: A geodetic graph is one in which every pair of its vertices has a unique path of shortest length.
As mentioned before, Ore [9] posed the question of characterizing geodetic graphs, which is still unresolved.

Characterization, enumeration and the general classification of geodetic graphs are open problems that have become a very important research topic due to the fact that geodetic graphs can be applied to the solution of other relevant problems in computer science [1, 2, 3].

accepted.question_text: Let G be a graph homeomorphic to the Petersen graph. If each path in G made of two successive segments is a geodesic, each cycle of G containing five segments has odd length, and all cycles of G containing six segments have equal length, are these three conditions not only sufficient but also necessary for G to be geodetic?

evidence.quote: It is known that the following three conditions are sufficient for a homeomorphic graph G to the Petersen graph to be geodetic:
(1) Each path composed of two successive segments, one followed by the other, is a geodesic in G.
(2) Each cycle of G containing five segments has odd length.
(3) All cycles of G containing six segments have equal length.
It is conjectured that the three conditions of each of the two previous statements are not only sufficient, but also necessary [6].

accepted.question_text: Let G be a graph homeomorphic to a Moore graph of diameter d and degree k >= 3, with the Moore graph distinct from K_n for n >= 5. If each path of G composed of d successive segments is a geodesic, each cycle of G containing 2d + 1 segments has odd length, and all cycles of G containing 2d + 2 segments have equal length, are these three conditions not only sufficient but also necessary for G to be geodetic?

evidence.quote: More generally, the following three conditions are sufficient for a homeomorphic graph G to any Moore graph of diameter d (k  3) distinct from Kn, n  5, to be geodetic:
(1) Each path of G composed of d successive segments, one followed by the other, is a geodesic in G.
(2) Each cycle of G containing 2d + 1 segments has odd length.
(3) All cycles of G containing 2d + 2 segments have equal length.
It is conjectured that the three conditions of each of the two previous statements are not only sufficient, but also necessary [6].

accepted.question_text: Can it be proved rigorously that the total number of geodetic graphs of diameter d >= 2 that are homeomorphic to the Petersen graph is (d + 3)C5, meaning the number of combinations of d + 3 elements taken 5 at a time?

evidence.quote: 1. Can be proved rigorously that the general number of all geodetic graphs of diameter d  2 homeomorphic to the Petersen graph is (d + 3)C5 (the number of combinations of d + 3 elements taken 5 at the time)?

accepted.question_text: Is it possible to devise a computer program that runs on a modern computer in real time, enumerates all natural solutions of the geodetic system of Diophantine equations associated with the Hoffman-Singleton graph, and thereby generates and determines the general number of all geodetic graphs of diameter d >= 2 that are homeomorphic to the Hoffman-Singleton graph?

evidence.quote: 2. Is it possible to devise a computer program to be run in a modern computer in real time that allows to enumerate the set of all natural solutions of the geodetic system of Diophantine equations associated with the Hoffman-Singleton graph and to generate and find the general number of all geodetic graphs of diameter d  2 homeomorphic to it as was done for the Petersen graph in [6]?

accepted.question_text: Do the geodetic systems of Diophantine equations associated with K4, the Petersen graph, and the Hoffman-Singleton graph share a hidden common structure in the distribution of their variables that would make it possible to construct the corresponding system for generating every geodetic graph homeomorphic to the still-undiscovered Moore graph with k = 57, including that graph itself?

evidence.quote: 3. Does there exist any sort of hidden structure contained within the distribution of the variables of the geodetic system of Diophantine equations associated with K4, the Petersen graph, and the Hoffman-Singleton graph that is common to the three systems and allows to construct the system to generate the class of all geodetic graphs homeomorphic to the undiscovered Moore graph (k = 57) including itself?

accepted.question_text: Do there exist infinitely many strongly regular geodetic graphs, or any strongly regular geodetic graphs that are not Moore graphs?

evidence.quote: 4. Do there exist infinitely many strongly regular geodetic graphs, or any strongly regular geodetic graphs that are not Moore graphs?

accepted.question_text: How does changing the topology of connections in a computer network influence the quality of network performance when the network is modeled by geodetic graphs, especially in terms of systemic hierarchy, diameter, vertex connectivity, reliability, cost, flexibility of topological change, and the number of graphs of a given diameter that represent the same network topology?

evidence.quote: An open problem is to research how the change of topology of connections influences the quality of network performance.

That quality of work can be significantly improved by changing the topology of connections, which in the case of homeomorphism can be done by knowing the exact number of graphs of given diameter d that represents the same network topology [5].

Discrete optimization, which is defined as a mathematical discipline that comprises not only combinatorial optimization, but also general (mixed-)integer optimization problems with no special combinatorial structure, and graph enumeration are theoretical topics very close related to the applied problem of creating complex computer networks of optimum performance, that is, computer networks with optimum indices of their operation quality such as systemic hierarchy, diameter, vertex connectivity, reliability, cost, and flexibility of topological change, among others [4, 5].

accepted.question_text: Can one determine a single model together with an adequate optimization technique that simultaneously accounts for many different characteristics of computer-network operation quality?

evidence.quote: Another open problem consists in determining a single model that enables to consider many different characteristics of the quality of network operation and an adequate technique to optimize them.

accepted.question_text: Let G be a locally-finite simple geodetic graph and let t be a natural number. If C is an embedded cycle whose diameter exceeds t and whose length is minimal among all such paths in G, must C contain a geodesic subpath of length t + 1?

evidence.quote: It is known that the general classification problem of geodetic graphs is related to the problem of the study of rewriting systems, which, at the same time, connects abstract algebra and theoretical computer science [2, 3]. As a result, a new contribution to a better understanding of the description of geodetic graphs consists in proving several conjectures, among them, the following one:

Let G be a locally-finite simple geodetic graph, and t ∈ N. If C is an embedded cycle of diameter exceeding t that has minimal length among all such paths in G, then C contains a geodesic subpath of length t + 1.

needs_review.question_text_raw: A couple of open problems are posed regarding the problem of finding the number of crossings of minimal length paths (geodesics) in a geodetic graph.

evidence.quote: Finally, a contribution to a better understanding of the structure of geodetic graphs applies mathematical methods of graph drawing to the problem of finding the number of crossings of minimal length paths (geodesics) in a geodetic graph. A couple of open problems are posed regarding this issue [1].
